title: Four better handoffs · fictional sample month
notes: SYNTHETIC TRAINING INTERVIEW. These four original sections were written for this software demonstration. No real expert, customer, endorsement, measured improvement or external delivery is represented. Replace with authorized client material before use.
interview:
Start a request with facts, not guesses
A useful work request begins with a small set of facts: what needs to change, who will use the result, the source material, and the date that matters. When a measurement or decision is missing, write down the question rather than quietly filling the gap.
Our fictional workshop uses a simple intake card. The card separates supplied facts from assumptions, links the original request, and gives unresolved questions an owner. The point is not to make every request longer. It is to make the next action clear.
Try it on one request this week. Highlight the facts you can trace to the source. Circle the decisions you still need. Send one consolidated clarification rather than several disconnected guesses. Keep the original wording beside your working summary so a later edit does not erase the starting point.

Make the next piece of work visible
A queue is useful when people can tell which request is active and what follows it. In this fictional workshop, we keep a short ordered list and explicitly mark one item as the current production request. A new request joins the queue; it does not silently replace the work already underway.
A visible queue also gives revision requests a home. Decide whether a revision belongs to the active item or needs its own slot. Record that choice next to the request, along with the source material and the expected output.
This week, write the next action for the active request as a sentence beginning with a verb. Then review the first item behind it. Does that item have the information needed to begin? Ask for missing material now, without pretending it is already in production. The queue should describe the work, not manufacture certainty about turnaround.

Review a change against the same starting point
A revision is easier to discuss when the original and the changed version remain available. Save the starting draft, record the requested change, and compare the result against that request. A broad instruction such as “make it better” needs a concrete conversation about the intended audience and purpose.
Our fictional workshop names revisions in order and keeps the source material attached. When a factual source changes, the affected copy returns to review. A previously approved sentence is not automatically approved against a different source.
For the next revision, ask three questions: what changed, why did it change, and which source supports the current wording? Keep comments tied to the passage they describe. Before handing over the result, check that the change did not remove a required detail elsewhere. The version history is there to support editing, not to substitute for the reader's judgment.

A finished file still needs a delivery handoff
Producing a file, importing it into another tool, scheduling it, and delivering it are different actions. Treat each as its own step. A newsletter ZIP on your computer is not a sent newsletter, and an editorial calendar reminder is not a job in an email platform.
In this fictional workshop, the handoff names the current revision, includes editable HTML and plain text, and states the intended UTC date. The operator then checks sender details, audience preferences, unsubscribe controls, and the platform preview before scheduling there.
Use the handoff to make the remaining work visible. Tell the next operator what is included and what still needs to happen. Record a delivery result only after the destination provides one. For this sample, the result is four editable newsletter issues and their source material. There are no subscribers, campaigns, payments, or delivery claims behind the example.
